title: A Restricted Boltzmann Machine with Quantum-State Visible Units
authors: Zhe-Hao Zhang, Yi-Cong Yu, Xiaoming Cai, Hai-Qing Lin
abstract: We construct a restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) whose visible input is a quantum state rather than a classical configuration. Each hidden unit carries a trainable quantum template prepared by a parametrized circuit and converts its overlap with the input into a feature. Treating quantum states as high-dimensional continuous visible objects creates nontrivial normalization and scaling problems. We regularize the continuous likelihood and derive two controlled high-dimensional limits, yielding a Hopfield-type network with continuous Hilbert-space patterns and a data-augmented Gram likelihood. The resulting algorithms are compact and use trainable circuit-prepared templates as measurement intermediaries between quantum data and classical optimization. Numerical simulations across several many-body systems demonstrate effective quantum-phase recognition and multicomponent feature extraction.
summary: This paper adapts the Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) to accept quantum states as input, overcoming the mathematical difficulties associated with continuous quantum variables. By deriving controlled high-dimensional limits, the authors create robust algorithms that successfully map complex quantum many-body states onto trainable feature representations. This demonstrates a powerful ML tool for analyzing quantum phase transitions.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of constructing a Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) where the visible input is a quantum state, rather than a classical configuration.
main_result: The authors derive two tractable, controlled high-dimensional limits—a Hopfield-type network and a Gram likelihood objective—allowing the RBM to perform quantum-phase recognition and feature extraction.
method: The core method involves regularizing the continuous likelihood integral over the quantum state space using spherical convolution and deriving specific high-dimensional limits to make the optimization tractable.
model_or_system: The model is a quantum-state visible RBM. It is benchmarked across several 1D quantum many-body systems, including the Aubry–André model, Bose–Hubbard model, and transverse-field Ising chain.
key_observables: Feature extraction capability, state recognition across quantum phase transitions, and the resulting coupling/Gram matrices ($J$ or $G$).
important_parameters: The high dimension $d$ of the visible space, and the controlled scaling factors ($\kappa_j$) used in the high-dimensional limits.
main_assumptions: The primary difficulty is the ill-posed nature of the continuous likelihood integral, which necessitates deriving controlled high-dimensional limits.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically shows the RBM structure, linking the quantum state input to the derived Ising and Gram model forms. Figures 2 and 4 compare the RBM's feature representation against standard physical diagnostics and PCA for various quantum models.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the quantum-state RBM and its inherent mathematical difficulties. It then derives and analyzes two controlled high-dimensional limits (linear/Hopfield and quadratic/Gram). Finally, it applies these derived algorithms to benchmark quantum many-body systems to demonstrate physical feature extraction.
why_interesting: This work provides a novel machine learning framework to analyze quantum many-body physics by mapping complex quantum states onto trainable, classical optimization objectives, which is highly relevant for understanding quantum phase transitions.
